Article Title: Devdutt Padikkal's 199 in vain as bad light forces draw in India A vs New Zealand A first unofficial Test
Article Text:
Image credit: X

India A fight back after first-innings collapse

Padikkal leads India's fightback

India A fall just short

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India A came agonisingly close to victory but had to settle for a draw against New Zealand A in the first unofficial Test after bad light brought an end to play on Day 4 in Lincoln on Tuesday.New Zealand A were 187/9 in their second innings while chasing a target of 313 when the umpires stopped play due to poor light. India A needed just one more wicket to win, but the conditions did not improve and the match eventually ended in a draw.Curtis Heaphy stood firm for the hosts, remaining unbeaten on 90 off 187 balls, with Jayden Lennox on six. The pair frustrated the Indian bowlers during the final session, helping New Zealand A survive until the close.India A had a difficult start to the match after being bowled out for just 113 in their first innings. Yash Rathod top-scored with an unbeaten 44, while Devdutt Padikkal made 32. Simon Keene led the New Zealand A attack with five wickets, while Zak Gibson picked up three.New Zealand A responded with 317, taking a first-innings lead of 204 runs. Captain Rhys Mariu scored 76, while Dean Foxcroft contributed 51. Kristian Clarke added 42, helping the hosts build a strong advantage.Auqib Nabi and Anshul Kamboj took three wickets each for India A, while Akash Deep claimed two.India A produced a strong response in their second innings, scoring 516 to set New Zealand A a target of 313. Padikkal was the standout performer with the bat, scoring 199 off 248 balls, including 24 fours and three sixes. He shared a 215-run partnership with Sai Sudharsan, who scored 91, to put India A back in the contest. Yash Rathod also made an important contribution with 66, while Washington Sundar scored 52. Auqib Nabi chipped in with 38, and Akash Deep remained unbeaten on 25.Padikkal missed out on a double-century by just one run after being given out caught behind. His innings, however, helped India A turn the match around after their disappointing first-innings performance.Chasing 313 for victory, New Zealand A lost three early wickets, with Auqib Nabi striking twice in the opening overs before dismissing Matthew Boyle. The hosts were soon under pressure, but Foxcroft's 42 offered some resistance.Mukesh Choudhary dismissed Foxcroft, while Anshul Kamboj removed wicketkeeper Mitchell Hay. Washington Sundar then sent back Kristian Clarke before Padikkal made an impact with the ball, taking his maiden first-class wicket by dismissing Fraser Sheat. He later removed Zak Gibson to leave New Zealand A at 160/8.Akash Deep bowled Simon Keene for five, leaving India A just one wicket away from victory.However, Heaphy and Lennox held on as bad light stopped play at 187/9 after 65 overs.Auqib Nabi finished with three wickets in the second innings, while Padikkal claimed two. Akash Deep, Mukesh Choudhary, Anshul Kamboj and Sundar took one wicket each.The two teams will now turn their attention to the second unofficial Test, scheduled to begin on Saturday.
Article Summary: New Zealand A were 187/9 in their second innings while chasing a target of 313 when the umpires stopped play due to poor light. India A needed just one more wicket to win, but conditions did not improve and the match eventually ended in a draw. Devdutt Padikkal was the standout performer with the bat, scoring 199 off 248 balls, including 24 fours and three sixes.

Article Title: 'Not trying to reinvent the wheel': Luke Williams backs Mumbai Indians' core for WPL 2027 | EXCLUSIVE
Article Text:
Mumbai Indians head coach Luke Williams

Injuries, close games and the need for consistency

Harmanpreet stays on as captain

The auction: immediate needs and future options

Data has its place, but players need to trust their game

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mumbai Indians missed the Women’s Premier League playoffs last season after injuries and illness disrupted their combinations and close games slipped away. New head coach Luke Williams believes the franchise can return to contention without making wholesale changes to a side that has won two titles in four seasons.“Certainly not trying to reinvent the wheel,” Williams told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction from Adelaide.The Australian takes over from Lisa Keightley, who left after one season in charge. Keightley had succeeded Charlotte Edwards, who guided Mumbai to their inaugural WPL title in 2023. Williams knows Edwards from their time working in England’s women’s setup and arrives with a WPL title of his own, having coached Royal Challengers Bengaluru to the championship in 2024.He spent the 2026 season away from the competition, but when the Mumbai job became available, the prospect of returning to WPL - and working with Harmanpreet Kaur - appealed to him.“I was sort of, I guess, still a little bit surprised when it came about,” he said. “And from my end, I was extremely honoured and was interested straight away. Obviously, I've had some previous experience in the WPL. I had a year away from it last season and really missed being involved in the competition.”Mumbai are the two-time WPL winners, and Williams said the franchise’s record, along with the prospect of responding to a difficult campaign, made the role attractive.“The success that MI have had in all leagues, but also the WPL with two titles in the four years, was really exciting. And probably coming off a tougher year last year as well is a motivating factor to try and bounce back straight away and really compete for the title this year,” he said.Mumbai finished the 2026 league stage with three wins and five defeats, with Hayley Matthews missing the first three matches with a quad injury, while Nat Sciver-Brunt also dealt with illness. Harmanpreet scored 342 runs, Sciver-Brunt made 321, and Amelia Kerr took 14 wickets, but Mumbai could not convert enough individual performances into wins.Williams pointed to the difficulty of settling combinations in a tournament with only eight league matches. Mumbai lost close games, including their opening fixture against RCB, and had little time to recover from setbacks.“It looked like a challenging year with some injury and illness at different times. So trying to settle the combination down at different times is a big part of it. There were some close games, even the first game of the tournament against RCB. I think in this tournament where there's only eight games, close games are so important to try to get them to go in your direction. And try to win those crucial moments,” he said.“Still had a positive net run rate last year, I think. Mumbai and RCB were the only two teams to finish with a positive net run rate. So there's still a lot of positive signs. But just a couple of areas that we can hopefully have a bit of fortune with injury and illness. But also make sure that our processes, especially in the tighter games, are really clear and able to get over the line in those.”Williams does not intend to overhaul the team’s approach. He wants players to be clear about their responsibilities, while allowing for changes as their games develop between WPL seasons.“Primarily there's a lot to continue on with, I think, in terms of philosophy. But again, I guess [with] each player, it's a year between WPLs. So the players would have developed different things. So being really clear on their role within the side, where there might be some subtle shifts from different years with that,” he said.He pointed to the retentions as an indication of the franchise’s plans.“But again, in terms of the overall makeup, I think, or the composition, you could probably see from our retentions that we're keen to retain that core nucleus of the squad. But again, there may be some subtle changes to different roles and how we go about little bits and pieces. But certainly not trying to reinvent the wheel.”Harmanpreet will continue to lead Mumbai, even as her international captaincy has ended. She stepped down as India captain this month, having led the team to its first Women’s Cricket World Cup title in 2025.For Williams, Harmanpreet remains central to his plans at Mumbai. The two have spoken online and over the phone and met during his recent visit to India.“Harman is obviously such an integral part of MI as well as Indian cricket, obviously. And will continue in the captaincy role and has just a huge presence within the franchise. Is really strong with her thoughts and beliefs and we're really aligned in how we want to take the team forward for not only this year but hopefully years to come,” Williams said.He values her ability to combine an intense competitive streak with composure when making decisions under pressure.“She's able to, I think, mix a steely sort of competitiveness and desire and all those attributes that you want to see in a leader, with still having a calmness and a game knowledge and an ability to make really good decisions under pressure,” he said.“So I love the combination of the leader that's there and stands up and always wants to compete, but also at the same time is able to be really calculated in the decisions that they make.”The WPL auction takes place in Kochi on October 28. Mumbai have retained Harmanpreet, Matthews, Sciver-Brunt and Kerr among others, giving Williams an experienced core to build around.His priority is to find players whose strengths complement those already in the squad, while ensuring the team has options for different pitches and conditions.“It's making sure that each person has some strengths that we feel can, I guess, be accentuated in our program, that will match well with other players that we've got, I guess, depending on the conditions that we're playing in, we've got options for wickets, whether they're turning wickets or slow wickets or whatever conditions we face, we've got a number of options to be able to do that,” he said.The search will not be limited to players expected to start every game. Williams also wants signings who can put pressure on the first-choice XI and step in when needed.“So we're in a really good position, I think, with a strong nucleus, experienced nucleus, but I think that's probably the primary function of the upcoming auction is to really be targeted in some players that we think can add, whether that's in the starting XI or putting pressure on or be ready to go if an opportunity presents,” he said.With the current WPL auction cycle entering its final year, immediate contribution will carry weight in recruitment. Williams said the franchise would nevertheless consider younger players who could remain part of the squad beyond the coming season.“Primarily in the last year of a cycle, you probably do lean towards immediate outputs and what the person can do in the next 12 months. That's probably certainly the initial lens that you look at players through,” he said.“But again, having a look at young players that may be able to be part of the franchise for a longer period of time, certainly cast an eye over that and be aware of that. And depending on how the auction goes or the person and how it unfolds, we're certainly open to that option as well to add to our list.”Williams has coached in the WPL and Australia’s Women’s Big Bash League, worked with England’s women’s team and been part of a title-winning Southern Brave staff in The Hundred. Across those environments, he said, preparation and confidence in individual roles remain central.“A lot of the same things are about making sure that your teams are as well-prepared as they possibly can be, that they're really confident in their own roles and also their teammates and the style of play that you want to do and really trying to get an environment that's happy and people are really enjoying themselves,” he said.“There's some ups and downs in T20 cricket. So, having a group that's really supportive of each other, that understands that there will be those ups and downs and are able to bounce back quickly after a tough game or a tough over or a tough delivery at different times is so important.”He likes using data and analytics, but does not believe every player needs to be thinking about match-ups and statistics while batting or bowling. The information has to suit the individual.“There's certain players that obviously the actual data or which bowlers potentially to target or batters to target or different fields really works for them. That's a bit of information. For others, I think it needs to very much be in the background, and the clear focus needs to be on their own individual strengths,” he said.“It's almost the coaches and the support staff's role to put them into the positions where they're likely to have the most success rather than them having to think too much about whether they need to adapt. It's actually us taking that pressure on ourselves to put them in the positions where they're most successful.”Williams is keen to use the available information without complicating decisions for players in the middle.“I'm someone that I do like the data and analytics side of cricket, but also very mindful that it's still a game. You don't want to be complicating and it's a really hard game to play. So, certainly want the players to be really focused on just what their task is at that moment and not be worrying too much about numbers and all that sort of stuff because it's a hard enough game without a lot of the stuff,” he said.Williams has also watched the WPL’s effect on Indian women’s cricket over its four seasons. He pointed to the national team’s World Cup win and the growing willingness of players to take risks.“I'm very excited about Indian women's cricket and the direction that it's heading. Obviously, the WPL, we've had four seasons of it, and in those four years, India have won a World Cup. And so, I certainly think you can sort of see the fruits of the investment in the WPL,” he said.“I think year on year, just the bravery and the way that the players take the game on, the athleticism across all teams and in the field continues to grow and grow every single year. But I think if I was going to pick one thing with the WPL's growth, it's just been that really taking the game on and that bravery to take risks and those sort of things.”As he prepares for his first season in charge of Mumbai, Williams wants the players and staff to take pride in representing the franchise.“I really want the group to love what they're doing, to be so proud of representing MI and we're in such a fortunate position to be able to represent the franchise, to play cricket professionally and really want to inspire the next generation of players in India and hopefully for the Mumbai Indians,” he said.“So, I really want all of our group, whether it's our staff, our players, to be passionate about what they do, love the franchise and really enjoy ourselves because we're very lucky to do what we do.”
Article Summary: Luke Williams is the new head coach of Mumbai Indians. He replaces Lisa Keightley, who left after one season in charge. Mumbai missed the Women's Premier League playoffs last season. Harmanpreet Kaur will continue to lead the side as captain.

Article Title: Three days to deadline, guidelines issued for IOA's SOM nominations
Article Text:
New Delhi, Oct 10 (IANS) The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has begun its 2026 electoral process under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, with the Athletes’ Commission election scheduled for November 3 and the Executive Council polls set for December 5.

NEW DELHI:

Eight representatives to enter the IOA General Assembly

PT Usha

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) Electoral Officer (returning officer), Sanjay K. Srivastava, has issued guidelines for the Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit (SOM) elections, warning that nominations that fail to comply with the prescribed conditions will not be considered valid.In the document dated October 26, retired IAS officer Srivastava clarified the nomination procedure and issued a modified Form 2 for candidates seeking election as SOMs to the IOA General Assembly. The deadline remains October 30.The revised instructions place particular emphasis on the role of proposers and seconders, who must be members of the male or female SOM roster published by the Electoral Officer on October 23.An individual can propose or second one candidate in the male category and one in the female category. However, if the same person endorses more than one candidate in either category, the later nomination will be rejected. The instructions also state that a proposer or seconder cannot withdraw their name once the nomination has been delivered.The rules permit cross-gender endorsements: a male SOM can propose or second a female candidate, and a female SOM can do the same for a male candidate.The restriction is on endorsing multiple candidates within the same category, not on the gender of the candidate being nominated.The SOM election will determine eight representatives to the IOA General Assembly, comprising four men and four women. Under the IOA’s Sportspersons of Outstanding Merit Rules, 2026, one male and one female representative will subsequently be elected from among the eight to the IOA Executive Council.The SOM framework is designed to incorporate the experience of former elite athletes, including the current president PT Usha , into the governance of Indian sport. Candidates must satisfy the prescribed eligibility conditions, including Indian citizenship, being of sound mind, being between 25 and 70 years of age on the date of application, and having retired from active sport for at least one year before applying. They must also have represented India in an Olympic sport for which the concerned national sports federation or sports body is an IOA member.The next stages of the process will involve scrutiny of nominations, disposal of objections and publication of the final list of contesting candidates. Polling is scheduled for November 9, and will be conducted virtually, with detailed instructions to be issued separately.
Article Summary: The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has begun its 2026 electoral process under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025. The Athletes’ Commission election scheduled for November 3 and the Executive Council polls set for December 5. The SOM election will determine eight representatives to the IOA General Assembly.

Article Title: Virat Kohli's heartfelt post for 'friend' Harry Kane after Ballon d'Or win
Article Text:
Virat Kohli and Harry Kane

What did Virat Kohli say to Harry Kane?

Kohli set for New Zealand ODIs

NEW DELHI: Virat Kohli on Tuesday congratulated Harry Kane after the England striker won the Ballon d'Or on Monday. Kohli shared a heartfelt message for his "friend", praising him for his hard work, honesty and determination throughout his football career.Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the prestigious award. The Bayern Munich striker had an outstanding season, scoring 73 goals for club and country and setting new scoring records in Germany.Kohli took to social media to congratulate Kane and wrote a beautiful post."Harry my friend, you deserve every bit of this award for your resilience, hard work and honesty with which you’ve carried yourself through all these years playing football at the top. Really happy for you. God bless you and your family. They must all be very proud of you as you would be of your own journey. My best wishes always. Congratulations @HKane," Kohli wrote.Kane finished ahead of several top players, including Lamine Yamal, Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi, in the voting for the men's award.Kohli will next be seen in action in India's five-match ODI series against New Zealand.The star batter heads into the series after an impressive show against the West Indies in September.Kohli scored 168 runs in three matches at an average of 84 and a strike rate of 155.55.He made an unbeaten 139 off just 88 balls in the opening ODI in Thiruvananthapuram, helping India secure a comfortable eight-wicket win. Captain Shubman Gill also played a key role, scoring 110 runs as India chased down the target with ease.During the innings, Kohli crossed 15,000 runs in ODIs, becoming only the second batter after Sachin Tendulkar to reach the milestone. His 55th ODI century was another reminder of his ability to dominate bowlers.India and New Zealand are scheduled to play five ODIs from November 4 to 15, 2026. The series will begin in Auckland, with the next matches scheduled in Wellington and Hamilton. The final two ODIs will be played in Mount Maunganui.
Article Summary: Virat Kohli congratulates Harry Kane on winning the Ballon d'Or. England striker became first Englishman in 25 years to win the prestigious award. Kohli praised Kane for his hard work, honesty and determination throughout his football career. India's star batter will next be seen in action in five-match series against New Zealand.

Article Title: 'That was his superpower': Faf du Plessis reveals what made MS Dhoni special
Article Text:
MS Dhoni (left) and Faf du Plessis (TOI Photo)

MS Dhoni's IPL future hinges on fitness

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you believe is MS Dhoni's greatest strength as a leader? Instinctive decision-making Calmness under pressure Ability to motivate players 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Former South Africa captain Faf du Plessis has offered an insight into what made MS Dhoni stand out as a leader during their time together at Chennai Super Kings (CSK), highlighting the former India captain's instinctive approach to the game and his ability to remain calm under pressure.Du Plessis spent nine seasons with CSK before joining Royal Challengers Bengaluru in 2022. Across 154 IPL appearances, he has scored 4,773 runs and won three IPL titles during his time with the Chennai-based franchise. Reflecting on his experience of playing under Dhoni , the Proteas batter explained how the wicketkeeper-batter's ability to read situations and respond instinctively influenced his own approach to captaincy.Speaking on the Prakhar Gupta Podcast, Du Plessis said Dhoni preferred to assess circumstances as they unfolded rather than rely heavily on plans made before a match."This guy has an incredible understanding of the game on the field. He doesn't like to plan too much beforehand and prefers to be instinctive during the match. That was his superpower. He would read the game and the players while staying remarkably calm, as everyone knows he is a very composed person.That's something I want to take from him and apply to my own captaincy," said Faf.While Du Plessis has reflected on the lessons he learnt from Dhoni, uncertainty continues to surround the former CSK captain's playing future. Dhoni has expressed his desire to feature for the franchise in the next IPL season, but has made it clear that his fitness will determine whether he can continue.Speaking at an event recently, Dhoni said he would assess his physical condition before making a final decision on his participation.“You will know before December,” Dhoni said. “Doc, I will have to go through the test. You will have to give me the report, and then before December, I will have to see, you know, how strong I am to maybe play one more season.”The wicketkeeper-batter, who will turn 46 next year, missed the entire IPL 2026 season because of recurring injuries. His potential return remains a significant talking point for CSK, who have struggled to recapture their earlier success in recent seasons.Dhoni stepped down as captain in 2024, handing over the leadership to Ruturaj Gaikwad . Since then, CSK have failed to reach the playoffs, finishing fifth, tenth and eighth in the points table across the three seasons.Dhoni also responded to the possibility of being unable to continue playing, using humour to underline the importance of getting his fitness right.“And if I am not (fit enough), then, you know, you will have to make sure that you do everything right with me and make sure that this old vintage vehicle is running well on the road. So all the pressure is on them,” Dhoni added, with a hint of light-heartedness, as he often does while responding to questions about his future.CSK's management has previously indicated that the decision rests with Dhoni himself. However, the franchise is also preparing for a major overhaul ahead of the next season, with long-time coach Stephen Fleming departing and Zaheer Khan taking over as his successor.Dhoni's role in the revamped set-up remains uncertain. Whether he returns to the field as a player or takes on a role away from it will depend on his fitness assessment and the decision he makes before December.
Article Summary: Faf du Plessis reveals what made MS Dhoni stand out as a leader. Former South Africa captain highlights Dhoni's instinctive approach to the game and his ability to remain calm under pressure. Dhoni has expressed his desire to feature for Chennai Super Kings in the next IPL season. The wicketkeeper-batter missed the entire IPL 2026 season because of recurring injuries.

Article Title: 'I feel proud of myself': Basketball player Pushpa Senthil Kumar's journey from learning to leading
Article Text:
Pushpa

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Nearly a decade ago, Pushpa Senthil Kumar stood at the Sree Kanteerava Indoor Stadium here, grappling with the nerves of captaining an Indian team for the first time. On her return to the same venue, she was no longer the uncertain teenager seeking guidance, but a 25-year-old leading Indian Railways against Asia’s best. The results were disappointing, with her team losing all three matches in the FIBA Women’s Basketball League Asia, but the return offered a moment to reflect on how far she had come.She had represented India at the U-16 level at the venue in 2017 and remembers the nervousness of captaining a team at that age, as well as the support she received from coach Zoran Visic. He helped her navigate an environment where communicating with teammates and coaches was challenging, and now she is a more confident skipper.“I feel proud of myself because the coaches believed in me. I was young and nervous back then. But my coach always backed me and turned me into a confident player and leader. And now, I am more experienced, and I trust my players and give them confidence. When we are low and feel like giving up, I support my teammates,” she told TOI.That confidence was hard-earned. Growing up in Mudikandanallur, a village in Tamil Nadu’s Nagapattinam district, Pushpa initially took up netball at a Sports Authority of India hostel in Mayiladuthurai, alongside her elder sister Sathiya.When netball opportunities dwindled, she turned to basketball. What began as a change of sport eventually led to a career and a place on the national team.Her international career began at the 2017 U-16 Women’s Asia Championship Division B, where she averaged 13.2 points and 13.2 rebounds. She moved to the U-18 team the following year and then made her senior debut at the 2021 Women’s Asia Cup Division A. At the 2025 Asia Cup Division B, she averaged 14.2 points and 6.6 rebounds, establishing herself as one of India’s key players.Off the court, sport also brought financial stability to her family. After her father’s death, her mother worked in a garment factory to support her daughters. Pushpa secured a Railways job in 2019.“I told my mother that I would take care of her because of our family situation, and the sport and Railways have helped me fulfil my responsibilities,” she added.As captain of a young team, Pushpa is equally conscious of the responsibility she carries. Seeing many youngsters come in, she wants the next generation to approach the game with greater belief and determination. “We have to focus and believe in ourselves,” she said.Her ambition is straightforward: to see India win more often. She believes the defeats in Bengaluru should serve as lessons, not setbacks, and adds, “I want us to win more. Women’s basketball has been going down, and we have to improve.”For a player who once arrived at the venue unsure how to lead, the journey has shown growth, responsibility, and belief, leaving her determined to help India win more often and turn lessons into results.
Article Summary: Pushpa Senthil Kumar captained Indian Railways at the FIBA Women's Basketball League Asia in Bengaluru. The 25-year-old had represented India at the venue at the U-16 level in 2017. She remembers the nervousness of captaining a team at that age.

Article Title: No sponsor, a career-threatening setback and one big dream: Nayanika Sanga’s story
Article Text:
Nayanika Sanga (Insta)

NEW DELHI:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For Nayanika Sanga, golf has always been about more than the scorecard. As the 22-year-old from Gurugram prepares to compete at the Women’s Indian Open from Oct 22-25 at the DLF Golf and Country Club in Gurugram, she is drawing on lessons learnt over years of competition, international exposure and a difficult comeback from injury. Her approach is simple: concentrate on what she can control, appreciate the opportunity to play and treat every round as a fresh challenge.The philosophy reflects a maturity that has developed through experience. Having travelled abroad for tournaments, including competing in France, Nayanika has learnt to approach the demands of professional golf with greater perspective.“When you play in India, it is like a family. You feel at home and at ease. But when you play outside, the environment is different. People are new, and there can be a language barrier. I think that has made me a little more resilient. When I compete back home now, I feel comfortable because I know the place and the people,” she said.Her journey began when she was five. Her father, who serves in the Navy, wanted her to take up a sport, believing it would help her develop as an individual. She tried squash, tennis and golf, but the response to her natural ability with a club encouraged the family to pursue the latter.Competition soon followed, and the game became a defining part of her life.One of the earliest milestones arrived when she was 11, winning the Kazi Cup at Willingdon Club in Mumbai.“That was definitely a life-changing experience because that was my first win as a child, a big win as a child. Once you start winning, it reinforces that feeling that you want to keep chasing it again and again,” she said.The road since then, however, has not been without setbacks. A wrist injury four years ago came at a particularly difficult time, when she had just turned professional and was playing well. Gratitude journalling became an important part of that process.“When I started playing again, I began focusing on smaller things and feeling grateful that at least today I can play, and tomorrow I can compete. Instead of thinking, ‘I need to win today’, being grateful for the small things in life has definitely helped me,” she said.Physical conditioning has also played a significant role in her return. A professional golfer’s workload extends beyond the hours spent practising and playing. Frequent travel, tournaments scheduled close together and the physical demands of carrying her own bag at overseas events can take a toll. Nayanika credits her strength and conditioning coach, Shaurya Sinha, with helping her rebuild confidence in her body and handle the demands of the circuit.“Because of fitness, I have been a little more resilient to injuries. Other than the injury I had four years ago, I have not had any issues, and I feel my fitness routine is what gets me going every week,” she said.The Women’s Indian Open will present another test. Nayanika regards the DLF Golf and Country Club course as challenging, but prefers to see its demands as an opportunity rather than an obstacle.“I think it is challenging in a fun way. I do not see the course as challenging; rather, every day will be a new challenge there. It will be fun to tackle a new challenge every day,” she said.That outlook also shapes how she approaches a field featuring accomplished players. Rather than becoming preoccupied with the reputations of her opponents, she wants to learn from them while remaining focused on her own performance. She relies more on feel and instinct than data when making decisions on the course, trusting her judgement when she believes her game is in good shape.Nayanika has also witnessed the growth of women’s golf in India. When she first turned professional, she recalled fields of around 30 to 35 players. This year, she said, the numbers have risen to approximately 60 to 62, reflecting greater interest among younger golfers in pursuing the professional route. Lower scores and more opportunities to compete overseas have contributed to the improving standard.Yet the growth of the game has not removed one of its persistent challenges: funding. Despite competing abroad and continuing to develop as a professional, she is still looking for a sponsor. Coming from a middle-class family, with her father serving in the Navy, she knows the financial demands of sustaining a career on tour.“It has been tough. My parents have sacrificed so much for me, and they continue to do so to support me,” she said.Her grandparents also travelled with her to tournaments when she was younger, stepping in whenever her father’s work commitments prevented him from accompanying her. Nayanika acknowledges their contribution.Away from golf, time with friends and playing badminton help her switch off from the constant demands of professional competition. She also looks up to Diksha Dagar and Aditi Ashok whose achievements have out Indian golf on the global map.Nayanika hopes her journey can encourage more young girls to pursue sport, particularly in a society where conventional career choices often dominate expectations.“If you fall in love with a sport, there is nothing better than that feeling. Parents should be willing to explore sporting opportunities when their children show interest and ability,” she said.As she heads into the Women’s Indian Open, her ambitions remain tied to the fundamentals she has learnt through experience: trust her instincts, stay patient and focus on the next shot. For a golfer who has learnt to find perspective in adversity, the challenge is not simply to compete against a strong field, but to keep moving forward, one round at a time.
Article Summary: Nayanika Sanga, 22, will compete at the Women’s Indian Open from Oct 22-25 at the DLF Golf and Country Club in Gurugram. Her approach is simple: concentrate on what she can control, appreciate the opportunity to play and treat every round as a fresh challenge.

Article Text:
Equestrian Federation of India

New Delhi:

Yet another tale of administrative chaos and athletes paying the price. Caught in a prolonged governance crisis at the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI), Indian riders now face a ban from international competitions, with their sporting futures hanging in the balance. The latest setback comes at a time when the govt is pushing to bring more international events to India and widen Indian athletes’ exposure to global competition.The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections, effectively shutting Indian riders, officials, trainers and horses out of international events. TOI is in possession of FEI’s Oct 15 letter confirming the decision, which was taken at the international body's board meeting on Oct 13.Explaining its move, the FEI said the EFI’s prolonged governance crisis had reached a tipping point. “The absence of elections to date to elect a new Executive Committee, has resulted in a prolonged governance and leadership irregularity that is no longer sustainable,” the letter by FEI Governance Director Francisco Lima stated.The crisis follows the Delhi high court’s dissolution of the EFI executive committee in Feb 2026. Its elected tenure had expired in Sept 2023, while fresh elections remain pending nine months after the court’s intervention. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) constituted an ad hoc committee on March 27 to oversee the federation and facilitate the electoral process.While acknowledging the committee’s Sept 27 submission and its work, the FEI said elections were expected by Jan 31, 2027. However, the suspension will be reviewed only after the polls are held and evaluated by the international body.The consequences are sweeping. Citing its statutes, the FEI said the EFI “may not attend or be represented at any session or meeting of any FEI body, nor may it organise international events.” More damagingly, athletes, officials, trainers and horses “may not participate in international events organised by the FEI or any other national federation, whether under the Indian flag or the FEI flag.”With the suspension taking effect before the stated election deadline, Indian riders risk losing crucial international competition opportunities. Their return will depend on the completion of elections and the FEI’s subsequent evaluation, leaving athletes caught in a governance crisis they did not create.
Article Summary: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections. Indian riders now face a ban from international competitions, with their sporting futures hanging in the balance. The latest setback comes at a time when the govt is pushing to bring more international events to India and widen Indian athletes' exposure to global competition.

Former Australia captain Steve Smith has been cleared of concussion and resumed fielding duties on the fifth day of the first Test against South Africa at Kingsmead in Durban on Tuesday, after undergoing a series of clinical assessments following a blow to the helmet.The 37-year-old batter was struck by a short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje during Australia's second innings. Smith attempted to duck under the ball but misjudged its trajectory as it failed to rise as much as he expected.Although he continued batting after the incident, scoring 27 off 41 balls before being caught at long-on off Simon Harmer, Smith did not take the field when South Africa began their second innings on Monday. A scoring error has triggered a major controversy in a Women's Under-19 cricket match between Jharkhand and Uttarakhand in Nagpur. However, the JCA has claimed that the match should have ended in a tie because a run was not added to Jharkhand's total.According to a report in The Indian Express, the controversy centres on an incident in the 30th over of Jharkhand's innings.One of the Jharkhand batters was run out while trying to complete a second run on the fourth ball of the over. However, the scorer did not change the decision.A Jharkhand official told The Indian Express that the missing run proved costly, as it changed both the result of the match and the team's tournament campaign.“The scoreboard at the far end had the updated score after each ball but the main scorer forgot to add one run which cost us a tie. As per the rule, umpires have to go by the scorer and not at the person doing scoring at the scoreboard,” a Jharkhand official told Indian Express.The JCA has now taken up the matter with the BCCI, alleging that the match ended in a tie but was recorded as a one-run defeat because of the scoring mistake.

Article Title: Shreyas Iyer’s India find their feet after turbulent T20I run, but Wellington brings a new test

The celebrations after India won the second T20I against New Zealand in Christchurch showed just how much the Men in Blue needed that result. Since winning the T20 World Cup, it has been a roller-coaster ride for the T20I team under new captain Shreyas Iyer , with India struggling to close out matches. It started on the Ireland tour, where India lost both matches while chasing, first by 34 runs and then by just one run.The poor form continued in the England series, where the hosts humbled India 4-0. This time, the team failed in both departments when it mattered.Ravi Bishnoi conceded 29 runs in the 17th over of the second match as the Three Lions cruised to victory with an over to spare.Then came a 76-run collapse as India slumped to their second-lowest T20I total in a 125-run defeat, their heaviest loss in the format. The struggles continued in the home series against the West Indies earlier this month, with the visitors eking out a 2-2 draw.The UK tour was an eye-opener, and Sanju Samson said after the first game against New Zealand that, with India playing non-stop cricket, the players had been “instructed” to keep their fitness levels high.The opener, who scored a 33-ball 67 in the opening game, said the team’s motto was to play an “aggressive” brand of cricket and that the mandate for the openers was to “kill the game in the Powerplay”.“Sometimes it comes off, sometimes it doesn’t, but we have to keep believing,” Samson said.Bowling coach Morne Morkel reiterated Samson’s message on the eve of the third T20I in Wellington, saying there was no option to slack off.“For us, it’s about playing a brand of cricket that is entertaining. We’re not always going to get it right. But it is about putting that aggressive foot forward. We had our challenges in England and Ireland, where we weren’t consistent. So, there’s a big focus on this tour, especially in white-ball cricket, to raise our standards and play a good brand of cricket,” Morkel said.India have been able to execute that aggressive approach in the first two games. They comfortably chased down 225 in the opener and then wriggled out of tight situations in the second match on their way to victory.First, the bowlers did well to restrict the Black Caps to 180. Then, after India were reduced to 70/5, Naman Dhir, Tilak Varma and Nitish Kumar Reddy kept their composure and used their cricketing smarts to guide the team to a four-wicket win.In Wellington, India will face an external challenge as they look to seal the series in windy conditions. On Monday, a wind warning was issued in the city, with the waterfront closed after several cyclists were knocked off their bicycles. Conditions are expected to improve by match time on Tuesday, but it will be chilly, and Morkel said the players must adjust.“This is a different beast, this wind. I was in the hotel this morning and the whole building was sort of shaking. It’s going to be a new thing that we add to our books for the guys to get used to and become accustomed to. But it’s about looking forward to that challenge and taking it head-on, and not making excuses,” he said.Meanwhile, teen opener Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will get another chance, with the injured Ishan Kishan ruled out of the third game as well.

That Nitish Kumar Reddy was one of only two players picked across all three squads for India’s tour of New Zealand speaks volumes about how highly the team management rates him. Recognising his potential, the team management has preferred him ahead of Shivam Dube since the third T20I against the West Indies. While he is not yet in the same bracket as Pandya, whose all-round skill set remains unmatched in India, Reddy has age on his side and continues to make strides with both bat and ball.His athletic fielding enhances his value.India bowling coach Morne Morkel believes Reddy possesses the attributes to become the all-format allrounder the team has long sought and could eventually develop into Pandya’s successor.Morkel recently described him as a player to “keep an eye on” and someone capable of producing a “magical ball” that can change the course of a game.Reddy is equally aware of the demands that come with the role.“The amount of work I have to do is more than anyone else, on and off the field,” he said after the second T20I.The Andhra cricketer first showcased his potential during India’s 2024-25 tour of Australia, where he marked his Test debut series with a memorable hundred at the MCG against a top Aussie attack.While his batting credentials were never in doubt, his bowling lacked the pace required to cement his place as a frontline allrounder. Determined to address that weakness, Reddy worked with fast-bowling and high-performance coach Steffan Jones ahead of the 2026 IPL.The improvement was immediate and visible. For a moment, Devdutt Padikkal could only stare in disbelief. One run short of a double-century, India's No. 3 was adjudged caught behind in contentious circumstances against New Zealand A in Lincoln. The dismissal ended a magnificent innings at 199, but not before the left-hander had sent a timely reminder of his ability to bounce back when it matters.After a disappointing outing against Australia A at home, Padikkal found his rhythm in the blustery conditions of New Zealand, producing a knock that could prove significant in his bid to strengthen his Test credentials.Ahead of India's two Test series against New Zealand, the 26-year-old spoke at length about a journey shaped by setbacks, self-doubt and evolution. From feeling underprepared for the challenge in Australia to rediscovering his game in Sri Lanka, Padikkal opened up about battling a prolonged illness in 2022, spending nearly two years trying to get back to his best, the technical adjustments he is making for New Zealand and the advice he received from KL Rahul Excerpts:It's been pretty good, to be honest. I've had a few sessions back home and played a couple of (India) A games against Australia A. Obviously, the conditions were different, but at the same time, it's important that you keep playing some red-ball cricket. Now, it's just about making a few adjustments, especially going to New Zealand, where it's going to be a different challenge compared to what we faced in Sri Lanka.The wind is something that's going to play a pretty major role, especially in Wellington. But at the same time, it's important that I don't make too many preconceptions. The India A games are key for us to really understand the conditions and get used to them as quickly as possible. So I'm trying not to look too much into it because it's very challenging to simulate what you would face there.I've watched a bit of the games that were played in New Zealand previously, and even the England series that took place there (2024). I think that was the last Test series that happened there [New Zealand hosted West Indies in December last year]. So I've watched a bit of that. But again, like I said, the conditions can be different when we go out there. It could be a different challenge for us, so for me, it's important that I adapt as quickly as possible.I practice things that I technically need to work on. I try to make sure that I'm playing the ball late, playing with the swing and trying to get those minute things right when I'm back home. Once I go out there, that's when I try to understand the conditions and then adapt to them.Every cricketer would have gone through something similar. They would have had that phase in their lives when they were trying to find answers. I think, for me, the last couple of years were about trying to understand where my game was at and what I needed to work on to really make sure that when I got that opportunity again, I was prepared.So that was the key for me. I feel that when I played that game in Perth, I was probably not ready. In terms of where my mindset was mentally and where my technique was, there were a lot of things I was still working on and still needed to get better at.Obviously, it was always going to be a challenging task to play that first game in Perth. I was up for it, and I was really excited about it. But now, looking back at it, I probably needed a lot more technical solidity to go out there and play against that level of bowling. Over the next two years, it was a phase in which I needed to understand that aspect of my game, try to figure out what I needed to do and how my game had to evolve to make sure that, eventually, when I got that opportunity in Sri Lanka, I was ready.I remember having a conversation with KL (Rahul) when I was in Australia about what I could do going ahead and what I needed to work on. The conversation was about just trying to evolve and getting better at your game every day.When you play at the highest level, it's easy to relax and think that you have made it or reached the pinnacle, that you don't need to work on too many things and just need to maintain that level. It's important to understand that everyone else around you is going to evolve. Everyone is constantly trying to get better. If you try to stay at the same level, it's going to cost you at the end of the day.So I think that's something that stuck with me. It was important that every game I played, regardless of whether it was at the Ranji Trophy level or the A team level, I performed better in the next game than in the previous one.That's how I looked at it. Every day that I went out to practise, it was important that I reminded myself to get better because it's not about maintaining the same level. It's about constantly upgrading.100%. Overseas tours are always a great experience, especially for someone young like me. It was important that I could go on those tours and learn different ways of playing, different ways of batting in different conditions and just evolve my game that way. But I think everything happens for a reason. It was unfortunate that I missed out, but I'm glad that eventually I got that opportunity.It's definitely not easy. I think you have to compartmentalise a lot when you switch formats. At the Ranji Trophy level, you still have seven to eight days of break between formats. You have time to prepare and try to switch formats, and that makes it a little bit easier.But at the same time, it's important that you try to keep those aspects of your game separate as much as possible. If you try to mix red-ball cricket and white-ball cricket together, it doesn't bring you a lot of success.I've been through that phase where I've tried to keep my technique very stable across the two formats. It's not always been easy. I've reached a stage in my career now where I've figured out how I can adjust and change my technique just enough to make sure that there's a clear difference in how I bat in both formats. The formats have become so specialised and people have gone up so many notches in each format, it's important that you continue to evolve that way if you want to play the white-ball game as well as the red-ball game. It's not the easiest thing to do, but it's something that I'm proud to be able to do at the moment.I think it's become a part of every cricketer's life in India. Everyone understands that there is a lot of competition. I don't think anyone feels really hard done by when someone else is picked over them because, almost always, that person deserves it too.So that's how it's been in Indian cricket over the last few years. We have so many talented cricketers, and everyone deserves to be at the highest level. But at the end of the day, only 11 can play. So sometimes someone misses out. It's always going to be a hard thing for that player.Everyone understands that everyone deserves to be there, and everyone understands their jobs. For me, it's no different. I've really enjoyed the competition. I've always felt that it gives me added motivation and a boost, and that's how I've always looked at it. As long as I'm pushing myself to get better, I think I'll continue to play.That was definitely the most difficult part of my life so far. It felt like things were against me. I thought this was probably going to be the end of my cricketing career because when you're out of cricket in India for a period that long, even if you miss one season, it feels like everyone else is miles ahead of you. To not be at my best for close to two years definitely felt that way.It definitely felt like I was not going to be able to get over this. But I'm really grateful and thankful to all the people who helped me through that phase: the doctors, the nutritionists and everyone who got me back to a stage where I could perform at the highest level again.That's the only thing I could think of when I was going through that phase. I just wanted to get healthy, get fit and make sure that I was playing cricket again. Eventually, once I got out of that phase, I was obviously doubly determined to get back to the stage where I felt I belonged.I think that was part of my journey, and it's something that I'm really grateful for experiencing because now I feel it's given me an added sense of gratitude whenever I get an opportunity to play for the country or my state. It makes me feel so blessed that I was able to get through that sickness and health issue and get back to playing on the field.
Article Summary: India's Devdutt Padikkal has had a roller-coaster journey in Tests. The 26-year- old opened up about battling a prolonged illness in 2022. He also spoke about the technical adjustments he is making for New Zealand. The India No. 3 also revealed the advice he received from KL Rahul.

That Nitish Kumar Reddy, being one of only two players named in all three squads for the New Zealand tour, speaks volumes about how highly India rate his skills.It has also provided the team management with an opportunity to develop an alternative to the often-injured Hardik Pandya , who is not getting any younger. On his part, the 25-year-old has made useful contributions to justify the faith shown in him.Reddy bowled his full quota of four overs in the first T20I in Christchurch and was entrusted with the responsibility of delivering the 19th over. He conceded 12 runs in that over and finished with a joint-best economy rate of 10, alongside Mayank Yadav.In the second game, he was once again handed the ball in the 19th over. This time, he conceded just 14 runs and claimed a wicket. The right-hander later returned to stitch together an unbeaten 69-run partnership off 30 balls with Tilak Varma to steer India to victory from a difficult position. He finished unbeaten on 26 off 13 balls.Those two performances are a testament to his ever-improving skills as an allrounder. The team think tank has recognised his potential and has preferred him over Shivam Dube since the third T20I against the West Indies. While he cannot yet be put in the same league as Pandya, whose skill set remains superior to that of any other Indian allrounder, Reddy has age on his side and continues to improve both aspects of his game, besides being an excellent fielder.India bowling coach Morne Morkel believes Reddy has the skills to become the all-format allrounder India have been desperately searching for and one who could eventually emerge as Pandya's successor.Morkel recently backed him publicly, stating that he is a player to "keep an eye on" and someone capable of producing a "magical ball" to unsettle batters.Reddy, too, does not shy away from questions about his credentials as an allrounder, nor does he shy away from putting in hard yards."The amount of work I have to do is more than anyone else, on and off the field," he said after the second game against New Zealand.Reddy made his Test debut during the 2024 tour of Australia and gave a good account of himself, including a century at the MCG against a bowling attack featuring Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon.While he showed what he could do with the bat, his bowling lacked the much-needed zip required to cement a regular place in the XI as an allrounder. He addressed that shortcoming by working with Steffan Jones, a former county cricketer and now a fast-bowling and high-performance coach, shortly before the 2026 IPL.The results were there for everyone to see. His pace consistently touched the mid-130kph range, a significant improvement from the mid-120s he had been bowling before his sessions with Jones.Reddy's biggest challenge, however, remains his fitness. He was set to travel to Zimbabwe for his maiden India call-up after the 2024 T20 World Cup, but a hernia injury scuppered those plans. Since then, he has spent considerable time on the sidelines with various injuries, including a freak gym accident in which he injured his left knee. Earlier this year, a quadriceps injury also ruled him out of the UK tour.With Reddy improving with every outing, the onus is now on the team management to use him judiciously and keep him fit and ready for the bigger challenges that lie ahead.

Article Title: Best ever! From 14 medals to 114: How India achieved more with fewer athletes at the Asian Para Games
Article Text:

From 14 medals to 114: India's remarkable rise

India's Asian Para Games record

Image credit: TimesofIndia.com

Athletics powers India's medal surge

India's leading medal-winning sports in Asian Para Games 2026

Multiple medallists underline India's depth

Paralympic progress provides the wider context

Fourth place sets a new benchmark

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

From 14 medals in 2010 to 114 in 2026, India’s remarkable rise continued in Aichi-Nagoya as a smaller contingent surpassed its previous best, achieved 30 gold medals and secured its highest-ever finish at the continental para-sport showpiece.India’s campaign at the Asian Para Games 2026 was a triumph that few would have predicted when the size of the contingent became known. With just 167 athletes travelling to Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the prospect of repeating the 100-plus medal haul achieved at Hangzhou in 2023 appeared ambitious. The previous edition had seen India send more than 300 athletes to the competition, returning with a record 108 medals after subsequent revisions to the original tally.But the Indian contingent defied expectations, producing an even bigger return with significantly fewer athletes. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place, both the highest medal tally and the best finish in the country's history at the event.The numbers tell a compelling story of progress. India improved its medal tally for the fifth consecutive edition, added to its gold-medal record and finished ahead of South Korea, which had threatened to challenge its position in the final standings.More than the record itself, the achievement highlighted how far India's para-sport movement has travelled in 16 years — from a modest 14-medal return at the inaugural edition in 2010 to a fourth-place finish among Asia's leading para-sport nations.India's progress at the Asian Para Games has been steady, with each edition bringing a new high in the overall medal tally.At Guangzhou in 2010, India won 14 medals — one gold, four silver and nine bronze — to finish 15th. The 2014 edition in Incheon brought a substantial improvement, with the country collecting 33 medals, including three gold, but remaining 15th in the standings.The breakthrough arrived at Jakarta in 2018. India's medal tally rose to 72, comprising 15 gold, 24 silver and 33 bronze, while its position improved to ninth.Hangzhou in 2023 marked another major leap. India crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time, initially returning with 111 medals before the tally was revised to 108 following a doping-related disqualification and a medal reallocation. The revised haul comprised 27 gold, 32 silver and 49 bronze, with India eventually classified sixth.Aichi-Nagoya extended that upward trajectory. India added six medals to its revised Hangzhou total, increased its gold-medal count from 27 to 30 and climbed two places to fourth.The numbers at a glance: India's medal tally increased more than eightfold between 2010 and 2026. Its gold-medal count grew from one to 30, while its position improved from 15th to fourth.The rise has not been limited to the overall tally. India has improved its standing in three successive editions since 2014, moving from 15th to ninth, then sixth and now fourth. The 2026 result represents the culmination of a sustained upward trend rather than an isolated breakthrough.The most striking feature of India's latest performance was the efficiency with which its athletes converted participation into medals.India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi-Nagoya. That was considerably fewer than the 309 athletes listed for the Hangzhou campaign in 2023, yet the team surpassed its previous best by six medals.The comparison is revealing. India sent approximately 46 per cent fewer athletes than it did to Hangzhou, but its medal tally increased by nearly six per cent. The gold-medal count rose by three, the silver tally by three, and the bronze count remained unchanged.On a simple medals-per-athlete measure, India's return increased from approximately 0.35 medals per athlete in Hangzhou to 0.68 in Aichi-Nagoya. This is an aggregate comparison, not an individual success rate, since athletes can win multiple medals and the number of events and opportunities varies across sports.Nevertheless, the figures underline the scale of the achievement. A smaller squad did not merely match the previous edition's success; it established a new benchmark for Indian para-sport.Para-athletics was the backbone of India's campaign, delivering 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. That represented nearly 57 per cent of the country's overall tally and made athletics the single biggest contributor to India's fourth-place finish.Para-badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze. Together, athletics and badminton accounted for 81 medals, more than 70 per cent of India's total.Swimming contributed 11 medals, comprising three silver and eight bronze. Archery added six medals, including three gold and three silver, while shooting produced five, with two gold, two silver and one bronze.Athletics' contribution also illustrates how India's progress has accelerated. At Hangzhou, para-athletics produced 52 medals, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 19 bronze. In Aichi-Nagoya, the discipline's haul rose to 65, with six additional gold medals.Badminton's contribution was different. India won 21 medals in the sport at Hangzhou, including four gold, but finished with 16 in 2026. Instead, the substantial gains in athletics and the contributions from other sports helped compensate for the decline in badminton medals.That distinction matters: the record haul reflects both the strength of India's established medal-winning disciplines and the need to broaden its success across events in future editions.India's record was supported by athletes who delivered more than once during the competition. A total of 26 Indian athletes won multiple medals, while six athletes collected multiple gold medals, demonstrating the importance of individual excellence in a campaign involving 11 sports.Archer Sheetal Devi was among the standout performers, winning two gold medals and a silver. Her two golds came in the mixed compound and individual compound events, while the silver added to her three-medal haul.Athletics provided several other multiple gold medallists. Dilip Gavit, Nishad Kumar, Pranav Soorma and Simran Sharma each won two gold medals, while shooting contributed through Mona Agarwal, who also secured two golds.Four athletes finished with three medals apiece: Sheetal Devi in archery, Thulasimathi Murugesan in badminton, Ravi Budigina in swimming and Himanshu Nandal in swimming. Their performances illustrated how athletes winning across multiple events can make a significant difference to a country's final tally.The figures also invite comparison with Hangzhou, where 25 Indian athletes won multiple medals. The increase to 26 in 2026 was modest, but the overall tally improved despite a much smaller contingent. The result points to a campaign in which medal-winning performances were concentrated among a relatively small squad.India's rise at the Asian Para Games has coincided with a significant improvement at the Paralympics, strengthening the country's standing in international para-sport.At Rio 2016, India won four medals and finished 43rd. Tokyo 2020 marked a breakthrough, with 19 medals — five gold, eight silver and six bronze — lifting India to 24th. At Paris 2024, India recorded its best Paralympic haul of 29 medals, comprising seven gold, nine silver and 13 bronze, to finish 18th.The progression at the Paralympics mirrors the broader trend at the Asian Para Games: larger medal returns, more gold medals and improvements in the standings.India's able-bodied contingent had also finished fourth at the 2026 Asian Games, although its 85-medal tally was below the 106 medals achieved at Hangzhou in 2023. The para contingent's performance offered a contrasting story of growth, with its medal count rising and its position improving.China dominated Aichi-Nagoya, finishing with 435 medals, including 207 gold. Hosts Japan were second with 186 medals, while Uzbekistan finished third with 145. India placed fourth with 114, ahead of South Korea, which collected 100 medals, including 29 gold.India's final position was not guaranteed until the closing stages. South Korea remained within reach, but its final-day return of one gold and two silver left it one gold behind India. The Indian contingent held on to fourth place with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze.The gap to third-placed Uzbekistan shows that further progress will require India to expand its medal-winning strength across disciplines. Yet the immediate achievement is significant: India has moved from 15th at the first two editions to fourth, while increasing its tally at every successive Games.The challenge now is to sustain that momentum, build a deeper pool of competitive athletes and reduce dependence on a handful of disciplines.For a contingent of just 167 athletes, 114 medals represent more than a record. They mark the latest step in a 16-year transformation of Indian para-sport — one that began with 14 medals in Guangzhou and has now culminated in a historic fourth-place finish in Aichi-Nagoya.
Article Summary: India fielded 167 athletes — 111 men and 56 women — across 11 sports at Aichi- Nagoya. India finished the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games with 114 medals — 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze — to secure fourth place. It is the best finish in the country's history at the event.

Article Title: The stars of India's surge: 5 standout performers of record Asian Para Games campaign
Article Text:
In this image received on Oct. 24, 2026, Double gold medallist Indian para-shooter Mona Agarwal carries the tricolour as India's flag bearer during the closing ceremony of the 5th Asian Para Games at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium, in Nagoya, Japan. (PCI via PTI Photo)

India returned from the Asian Para Games in Nagoya with its best-ever medal haul of 114 medals, powered by world records, golden doubles and medal-winning debuts. TOI picks out the ones who stole the show. .. MONA AGARWAL : A golden double and a world recordMona Agarwal won the women’s 10m air rifle standing SH1 gold before setting a world record in the 50m rifle three positions SH1. Her score of 357.5 secured a second title and made her the first Indian para-shooter to medal in the event. The Jaipur-based Paris Paralympics bronze medallist trained for the 50m event with a rented rifle, travelling long distances to train. PRANAV SOORMA : Two titles, two recordsPranav Soorma claimed the men’s discus throw F51/52/53 gold with an Asian-record effort of 11.66m, then added the club throw F51 title with a Games-record 32.87m. Paralysed after a spinal cord injury at 16, Soorma rebuilt his life through education and sport. His Nagoya double followed club throw gold at the previous Asian Para Games and silver at the Paris Paralympics. NISHAD KUMAR : Two disciplines, two gold medalsNishad Kumar ventured beyond his high jump speciality to win the men’s T47 long jump with an effort of 7.11m, then claimed high jump gold with a Games-record clearance of 2.04m.The double Paralympic silver medallist took on the additional discipline despite a troublesome knee, showcasing his versatility.SIMRAN SHARMA: Silver to goldSimran Sharma won the women’s 200m and 100m T12 titles, improving on her two silvers at the previous Games. The visually impaired sprinter from Ghaziabad followed her 200m triumph with a Games-record 12.02s in the 100m, finishing ahead of Iran’s Hajar Safarzadeh.SHEETAL DEVI: Golden comebackSheetal beat Singapore’s Nur Syahidah Alim in the women’s individual compound final. She also won women’s compound doubles silver with Payal Nag and mixed-team gold.FINAL BOWMona Agarwal with the Indian flag at the closing ceremony on Saturday.
Article Summary: India returned from the Asian Para Games in Nagoya with its best-ever medal haul of 114 medals, powered by world records, golden doubles and medal-winning debuts. Mona Agarwal won the women’s 10m air rifle standing SH1 gold before setting a world record in the 50m rifle three positions SH1.

Article Title: Asian Para Games bronze leaves Suhas Yathiraj hungry for gold amid IAS duties and badminton
Article Text:

Third Paralympics, one big dream: Gold at LA 2028

IAS officer by day, shuttler by night

NEW DELHI: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. Having beaten Indonesia's Fredy Setiawan in their group match just days earlier, the Indian shuttler had hoped to reach the final and fight for gold.Suhas lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23-21, 8-21, 15-21. He had chances to take the opening game but failed to convert them. After bouncing back to win the second game 21-8, he lost focus at a crucial stage of the decider.“Definitely not satisfied with bronze. I think if I had played up to my full potential, I would have definitely done better. In fact, I defeated Fredy of Indonesia in the group match in Nagoya only a few days ago,” Suhas told TimesofIndia.com from Aichi-Nagoya in Japan.“In the semifinal match, the first set was very close. I lost 23-21 and I had game point, set point, but I couldn't convert that. In the second set, I won very easily. In the third set, I think after 10-all, I sort of lost focus for two to three rallies. That is where he took the game. So, it was not my best day, I would assume. I would always love to win a gold medal. So, yes, I am a little sad from that angle,” he said.The defeat also reminded him of how important it is to perform under pressure at major tournaments.“It is the most important factor to win medals at major games because you might be training well, you might actually have the fitness and the skills. But if you don't recreate that during the major games, then probably it is of not much use in terms of professional success,” Suhas said.Suhas, an IAS officer, said he had never imagined representing India in international badminton a decade ago.In November 2016, he made his debut at the Asian Championships in Beijing and won gold. Since then, he has won several medals at major international events. These include bronze at the 2018 Asian Para Games in Jakarta, silver at the Tokyo 2020 Paralympics, another silver at the Paris 2024 Paralympics, gold at the Hangzhou Asian Para Games and bronze in Nagoya.The 43-year-old has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024, winning silver on both occasions.With the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics approaching, the big question is whether he can go one step further and win gold.The desire is there, but Suhas is not looking too far ahead. He wants to take things one step at a time.“If you had asked me 10 years ago, I didn't even know that I would play for India. But whenever I look at the medals and the love I have got from fans and sportspersons around the world, the journey has been quite satisfying. I have had the honour of wearing the Indian jersey and winning medals for my country,” he said.“I am grateful for what God has given me. I never imagined that I would become an IAS officer one day, an Arjuna awardee or a badminton player winning medals for India. I never imagined all this. But thanks to the Almighty for all these,” Suhas, who is also an Arjuna Award recipient, said.“So if God and destiny have been kind to me, I hope they will take me to a place that I deserve. I hope I can do the best that I can in whatever I choose to,” he added.For most people, the end of a hectic working day is a time to relax, spend time with family, play with their children or watch a movie.For Suhas, it is often time to pick up his badminton racket and head to the court. His day includes early-morning gym sessions, office work, inspections, meetings, video conferences and checking files. Despite his demanding responsibilities as an IAS officer, he makes time for badminton and follows a strict fitness routine to compete at the highest level.Balancing the two careers is not easy, but his love for the sport keeps him going.“If you choose what you love, then the journey becomes painless. You enjoy that journey. That's what I do,” Suhas said.Explaining how he manages his work and training, he said: “It is challenging. My training generally starts in the night and it always involves sacrifices. Probably others would be spending time with their family members or having leisure time. My leisure time is to play badminton. In badminton, you need an extremely high level of fitness. It's challenging, hectic but at the same time I love it.”“I don't remember eating sweets in the last many months. I can't recall when I had my last sweet. So, I almost don't eat sweets or fried food and am also quite conscious about the nutrition that I take,” he said.Suhas grew up watching Malaysian badminton great Lee Chong Wei and was inspired by his movement on the court.“Yes, I have always been inspired by so many top players in the able-bodied category. Growing up, I watched the matches of Lee Chong Wei and how he used to move around the court,” he said.“Even in India, the top shuttlers perform extremely well, whether it is Lakshya Sen, HS Prannoy or Kidambi Srikanth. I know them personally and have always admired how well they are able to compete at the top,” Suhas signed off.
Article Summary: Suhas Yathiraj was disappointed with his bronze medal at the Asian Para Games in Nagoya. The Indian shuttler lost the men's singles SL4 semifinal 23- 21, 8-21, 15-21. Suhas has represented India at two Paralympic Games, Tokyo in 2020 and Paris in 2024.

Article Title: Asian Para Games conclude in Nagoya: India sign off with record 114 medals, finish fourth
Article Text:
India finish fourth as China lead medal standings at Asian Para Games.

NEW DELHI: India signed off from the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Para Games with their best-ever medal haul of 114 medals as the week-long continental competition concluded with a closing ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletics Stadium in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday.Double gold medallists Nishad Kumar and Mona Agarwal led the Indian contingent as flag-bearers at the ceremony, marking the end of a landmark campaign in which the country's para-athletes delivered historic victories, world-record performances and podium sweeps across disciplines.India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games.Held in Japan for the first time, the fifth edition of the Asian Para Games brought together around 4,000 athletes and staff from 45 countries and regions. The competition featured 18 sports, with more than 20 world records reportedly set during the seven-day event.China topped the medal table with 435 medals, including 207 gold, while hosts Japan finished second with 186 medals — 64 gold, 60 silver and 62 bronze.Uzbekistan emerged as the third-ranked nation, collecting 145 medals, including 45 gold.India's fourth-place finish was particularly significant given the size of its contingent. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou.President Droupadi Murmu congratulated the Indian contingent on its record performance, saying the achievement reflected the athletes' hard work, perseverance and self-belief.In a post on X, Murmu said the unprecedented medal haul would inspire young people to dream big, work with dedication and remain positive in the face of challenges. She also extended her congratulations to the entire Indian contingent.Para athletics was India's biggest medal contributor, accounting for 65 medals — 22 gold, 19 silver and 24 bronze. Para badminton followed with 16 medals, including three gold, five silver and eight bronze.India also won 11 medals in para swimming, seven in para table tennis, six in para archery and five in para shooting. The contingent added two medals each in para judo and para powerlifting.The closing ceremony brought together athletes, officials and dignitaries to mark the conclusion of the Games. Asian Paralympic Committee president Majid Rashed declared the event closed, highlighting the growing strength of para sport across Asia and its role in building a more inclusive society.Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also praised the athletes' determination, teamwork and sportsmanship, describing their performances as a reminder of the “profound beauty” of para sports.The Asian Para Games began in Guangzhou, China, in 2010, evolving from the Far East and South Pacific Games Federation for the Disabled. The Aichi-Nagoya edition was the fifth staging of the event, with Doha, Qatar, scheduled to host the sixth in 2030.For India, the closing ceremony marked the end of a historic campaign — one that raised the country's medal benchmark and showcased the depth and growing strength of its para-sport movement.
Article Summary: India finished fourth in the overall standings with 30 gold, 35 silver and 49 bronze medals, surpassing its previous best of 108 medals at the 2022 Hangzhou Games. A total of 168 para-athletes represented the country at Aichi-Nagoya, compared with 309 at the previous edition in Hangzhou.
